I want to thank all the reviewers and authors for their work and for the discussion.

**Strengths:**

- All reviewers agreed that the empirical speedup compared to the current gold standard while maintaining comparable accuracy is impressive. I would add that crucial advances in the field of motor unit decomposition are fairly rare (as evidenced by the related work discussion in this paper) such that the step forward provided by this work weighs particularly heavy.
- While the topic of the approach (motor unit decomposition) is relatively niche, it is crucial in the clinical application context of neuro-prosthetic control.
- Multiple reviewers also mentioned the quality of the simulation studies (jo60 and 1GJy)

**Weaknesses:**

- Multiple reviewers were concerned by the low number of baselines. However, this was explained by the authors with specifics of the domain, limiting the number of matching baselines.
- Multiple reviewers mentioned that public data sets should also have been used to evaluate the model. The authors explained that this has the crucial drawback of lacking a ground truth (we do not know what the true spike trains would be).
- The user study was only performed with a single subject. However, with commendable effort, the authors recruited five additional subjects for the discussion period and presented additional results, consistent with the results reported in the paper.

Overall, the argument against public data set appears not quite convincing and such additional results would certainly have raised the empirical quality of the paper. However, the additional empiric results with healthy subjects provide (arguably) an even more convincing extension. As such, I still believe that acceptance is in order.
We would like to thank the reviewers for their time and comments to help improve the work. We would also like to thank the AC for facilitating the discussion.

**Synthetic data complexity:** We agree that testing algorithmic limits is important and have expanded our simulation studies to more challenging scenarios. We tested configurations up to n_chan/2 sources across all three methods:
- 32 channels: 5, 10, 15 motor units  
- 64 channels: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 motor units

These configurations span the physiologically realistic range for motor unit decomposition. Testing greater than n_chan/2 motor units would require additional computational time that exceeds the current author-reviewer discussion period timeline, though this represents an interesting direction for future algorithmic stress testing.

**Spiking neural network demonstration:** We respectfully maintain that this demonstration addresses a key clinical need. The demonstration shows practical feasibility in a motor-impaired population under real clinical time constraints where lengthy decomposition procedures are not viable, highlighting our work's translational impact. We understand this may be viewed differently and respect that perspective.

**Runtime comparison methodology:** We understand your continued concern about implementation specific factors affecting runtime comparisons. As previously detailed, we used standard optimized implementations without custom modifications on identical hardware to ensure fair comparison under realistic usage conditions.

We believe these additional data substantially address the concerns about dataset diversity and algorithmic evaluation while maintaining the core contributions of computational efficiency and practical utility demonstrated in our work.

I thank the authors for their detailed and thorough response to myself and the other reviewers. I think the comparison with other methods on simulated will aid in the completeness. I also thought some of the points around asymptotic analyses raised by jo6o (pt. 4,5,7) were good and would be important to include in the manuscript. As a result of this, I am happy to increase my score, but I also stand by opinion that I feel the paper is not sufficient to accept. 

Physiology is very different across individuals, and having a 1 participant evaluation dataset is simply insufficient. This alone is the most important issue. I also stand by the point that the synthetic data experiments are too easy -- the point of these should be to discover the noise level and conditions at which these algorithms break down, because all of these algorithms will break down in the limit of very high activity and sources. I still feel like the spiking NN does not add much to the manuscript. While i appreciate the responses about computational optimization of alternative methods, I am very hesitant to draw too much from the empirical observations of runtime improvements that could rely on implementation specific factors across algorithms. This could be improved by showing the runtime performance scaling compared to alternative methods, but these should have been included in the original submission.

I also want to note that there is concordance between my review and many of the other reviewers, e.g. jo6o, who notes the Simplified Task, limited algorithmic novelty and limited dataset diversity. I realize these reviewers feel differently about the overall score, but I index much more heavily on the limited evaluation presented.

Thank you for challenging our assumptions about decomposing more sources than channels. After testing scenarios where n_sources > n_channels, we found that reliable decomposition was not possible. This represents an underdetermined BSS problem where, despite the sparsity of motor unit spike trains, our method cannot overcome the constraint of having fewer channels than sources. When n_sources = n_channels, decomposition was technically possible but with a large increase in false positives, likely from incomplete source separation where sources remain partially mixed due to insufficient redundant information.

We will update the manuscript to clarify that the extend-lag procedure enhances source separability by capturing temporal dynamics and improves conditioning, but does not enable underdetermined decomposition.

Regarding method comparison, we tested MUelim, SCD, and MUEdit on identical simulated datasets (32 and 64 channels with 3, 4, 5, and 6 motor unit sources) and obtained the following performance:

### Comparison of MUelim with other methods
| Method  | Accuracy (%) (mean ± SEM) | False Positives (mean ± SEM per source) | False Positives (sum) | False Negatives (mean ± SEM per source) | False Negatives (sum) |
|---------|--------------------------|-----------------------------------------|----------------------|-----------------------------------------|----------------------|
| MUelim  | 99.93 ± 0.03             | 0.56 ± 0.19                             | 20                   | 0.22 ± 0.09                             | 8                    |
| SCD     | 99.91 ± 0.05             | 0.72 ± 0.22                             | 26                   | 0.28 ± 0.15                             | 10                   |
| MUEdit  | 95.92 ± 0.37             | 0.00 ± 0.00                             | 0                    | 12.22 ± 1.12                            | 440                  |

All methods successfully identified all sources across the 8 simulation scenarios. When comparing spike timings with ground truth spike samples, the results demonstrate that MUelim achieves comparable decomposition quality to SCD with very similar accuracy and error rates. MUEdit uses a more conservative approach, avoiding false positives entirely but at the cost of substantially higher false negatives and lower overall accuracy.

We appreciate your thorough evaluation of our work and will incorporate these updates in the revision.

We thank the reviewer for their thorough and constructive feedback, and for the many helpful suggestions to improve the manuscript. We are pleased that the reviewer found the work technically solid and well-motivated. 

Below, we address each question and outline the corresponding changes we will make to the manuscript. Regarding the main weaknesses identified by the reviewer: (1) simulation comparison and figure updates are addressed in questions 2 and 6, (2) online vs offline decomposition clarification is covered in questions 5 and 13, and (3) clinical task motivation concerns are discussed in question 10.

**1. Paragraph on how the MUAP waveforms are extracted (lines 181-186) is not very clear. Please add more details into how this process works.**

MUAP waveforms are extracted using spike-triggered averaging (STA), which involves averaging the EMG signal around detected spike times to isolate the average waveform associated with each motor unit. Specifically, our implementation performs the following steps: (1) For each detected motor unit spike timing, we extract a time window of configurable duration (default 30ms) centered around the spike impulse. (2) To improve waveform quality, we reconstruct the EMG signal from source space using the computed BSS inverse filters while suppressing other motor unit sources, which reduces cross-contamination between motor units. (3) To handle temporal jitter in spike detection, we align waveforms to their global maxima across channels to ensure consistent temporal alignment before averaging. (4) The algorithm extracts waveforms from all available channels, and for visualization purposes, we display results from the 5 most active channels based on signal amplitude. (5) Individual MUAP traces can be computed using a sliding window approach spanning subsets of detected spikes to show temporal evolution throughout the recording. This reconstruction-based STA approach is advantageous because it leverages the spatial filtering capabilities of the BSS decomposition to provide cleaner, less contaminated MUAP waveforms compared to traditional direct EMG averaging. We will add these technical details to the Methods section to clarify the MUAP extraction process.

**2. You mention in the introduction that the addition of time-delayed extensions prior to joint diagonalizations helps with potentially extracting more sources than channels. However, in section 2.3 you only evaluate cases in which there are many more channels than sources. What happens when the number of sources is higher than the number of channels? Also, please compare the simulation results you got with existing methods (such as MUedit and SCD).**

Thank you for this suggestion and catching an oversight on our part. The extend-lag procedure increases effective dimensionality from C channels to C×R extended channels, theoretically enabling extraction of up to C×R sources per BSS iteration. We will add simulation scenarios where the number of sources exceeds the original channel count to directly validate this key theoretical claim.

Regarding simulation comparisons, we acknowledge this limitation and agree that direct comparison on identical synthetic data would strengthen our evaluation. We will include results comparing MUelim, SCD, and MUEdit on identical simulated datasets to provide ground truth validation of relative performance.

**3. In section 2.4, please add how much residual movement the participant had available. Were they able to open and close their hand by themselves?**

The participant was able to partially open and close his hand, though not fully, and exhibited limited grip strength. Abnormal muscle synergies, particularly overactivity in the wrist flexors, limited his ability to achieve wrist extension. FES facilitated more complete hand opening, enhancing functional performance and reducing reliance on compensatory strategies. We will add this information to Section 2.4.

**4. The manuscript would greatly benefit from some diagram of the training procedure and inference during the neuroprosthetic experiment, potentially as an addition to Figure 3.**

We agree with the reviewer that a diagram would improve clarity. We will add a diagram illustrating the training and inference workflow for the neuroprosthetic experiment.

**5. Was the EMG decomposition done before starting the inference experiment? If so, how did you decompose the EMG signal in real-time? Please clarify. If you are pre-computing the forward filters, please clarify.**

The BSS forward filters are computed in-session (fit phase) after collecting a block of training data, then used for real-time inference (transform phase), following standard scikit-learn convention. The supplementary pseudocode shows these phases. We will clarify this procedure in the Methods section.

**6. Please add a figure to the main text with the results from the simulation experiment, as it can give key insights into whether the proposed method is working as expected. At the beginning of the results section you cite Figure 1, but that doesn't really contain simulation results.**

We will incorporate simulation experiment results from the supplementary materials into a figure in the main text, as suggested by the reviewer.

**7. Make sure that the units of Figure 2B (especially the right plot) are correct.**

Thank you for catching this. When combining figures with different axes, we mistakenly removed the units on the right plot. We will update the figure to ensure the units correspond appropriately to each axis.

**8. Figure 2C is not mentioned in the main text: what is the message you are trying to convey with it?**

Figure 2C shows the inverse BSS filters, which help to visually localize MU sources on the grid and assess their spatial properties. We will explicitly mention and explain Figure 2C in the main text.

**9. In Table 1, why do you show variability for MUelim but not for the other methods? Also, add a discussion on what the expected number of motor units should be, to better understand the results.**

Uncertainty was reported for MUelim because we ran the algorithm over multiple seeds for each parameter setting (main text, Sec. 2.3). For SCD, results were deterministic and for MUEdit, the manual nature of the tool precluded repeated runs. Regarding the expected number of motor units, the yield depends on the number of channels, muscle, and recording quality. In simulation and experimental studies (see Farina et al., 2008; Negro et al., 2016), typical yields for high-density grids in hand/forearm muscles are on the order of 10–30 unique motor units per contraction, with higher yields possible in ideal conditions. Our results are consistent with these expectations. We will add clarifying details to the text.

**10. How does the per-bin accuracy looks like if you use the full non-decomposed EMG rather than motor units? I would imagine that it would be much higher performance, but that would depend on how much residual movement the participant may have. Please add a few sentences to the limitations paragraph related to this method in this participant.**

We appreciate this suggestion to add to the manuscript. In an offline analysis trained using the same dataset used in session, our default RMS-NN pipeline achieved 86% bin-wise accuracy on the test set compared to the live 85% accuracy for the MU-SNN pipeline. Note that because FES was already triggered by the MU-based decoder live during the session, direct online comparison is not possible as we are evaluating the closed-loop response after FES has already been applied, which affects motor recruitment and subsequent EMG signals. With further SNN optimization, we could likely close this small gap, though this was not the focus of the work. As suggested by the reviewer, we will add this limitation to the discussion section.

**11. Mark the transition between rest and hand open in Figure 3A**

We will mark the transition between rest and hand open in Figure 3A as suggested by the reviewer.

**12. Figure 3D probably has wrong units.**

Thank you for catching this error. The units should be mV, not µV. We will correct this in the revised manuscript.

**13. "MUelim achieves similar or greater source yield with substantially reduced computation time, supporting its use in closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems". However, the computation times you show are in the order of minutes. If you are pre-computing the forward filters please clarify and tone down the claim.**

Thank you for this important clarification. Our method's fast BSS forward filter computation (minutes vs up to hours for existing methods) is what makes it well-suited for real-time applications. We will reference the supplementary pseudocode and update the text to make the fit/transform workflow clearer. We will revise this sentence to: "MUelim achieves similar or greater source yield with substantially reduced BSS filter computation time (minutes vs up to hours), enabling practical deployment in closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems where rapid session setup is required."

We thank the reviewer again for their positive assessment and helpful feedback, which will significantly improve the clarity and quality of the manuscript.

We thank the reviewer for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the novelty and computational efficiency of our approach. Our primary goal was to introduce and validate the MUelim algorithm, with the physiological example serving as a pilot demonstration of its practical utility. The main advantage of MUelim is its substantial improvement in computation speed for motor unit decomposition, enabling real-time applications that are not feasible with existing methods.

Below, we address the main points raised:

**1. Evaluations and baselines are unconvincing and limited. The advantages of the algorithm is not made especially clear, and its performance in different data regimes (e.g. sparse, dense, scaling with channel counts) is not shown. There is not a set of ablations that makes clear how different algorithmic properties and features factor into computational savings and data quality (e.g. removing time lag, approximations of joint diagonalization).**

We respectfully disagree and note that the manuscript provides both simulated and physiological evaluations with rigorous benchmarking: (1) comprehensive simulated data experiments (8 scenarios with 32-64 channels and 3-6 sources each), (2) physiological experiments on HD-EMG grid data, and (3) direct benchmarking against state-of-the-art methods using recommended parameters (Table 1 and Supp. Fig. S3).

Regarding ablations, we conducted four key ablation studies (Supp. Fig. S3) evaluating computation time and sources extracted: (1) time lag and (2) extension factor ablation showing the extend-lag procedure effect. When extension factor=1, the extend-lag procedure is effectively removed (same number of channels with no extension or time lag). (3) Bin size and (4) SPD matrix estimator comparison evaluating parameters that affect what matrices are used as input for joint diagonalization. While we focus on one joint diagonalization method, this was deliberate as evaluating different approaches has been extensively studied in prior work.

**2. The synthetic data experiments are too easy, as the algorithm achieves perfect performance. Competing methods are not benchmarked on synthetic data, which is the only regime that has a ground truth, so its unclear exactly how these are compared.**

We respectfully disagree that the synthetic data experiments are "too easy." The simulation scenarios were designed to include multiple sources, noise, and amplitude modulation, providing physiologically realistic scenarios. The high accuracy achieved reflects our approach's effectiveness on realistic EMG data, not oversimplified scenarios.

However, we acknowledge the reviewer's valid point about direct comparison on synthetic data. We agree that benchmarking all methods on identical synthetic data would strengthen our work. We will include results comparing MUelim, SCD, and MUEdit on the same simulated datasets in the revision.

**3. The proposed algorithm is benchmarked in Fig. 2 with extensive hyperparameter tuning as shown in Supp. Fig. 3 and then compared to alternative algorithms using open source hyperparameters. Its not clear if these hyperparameters were tuned on the evaluation set, and how the competing algorithms would perform with additional hyperparameter tuning.**

As shown in Supp. Fig. S3 and described in the main text (Sec. 3.1), the parameter sweeps for MUelim were not intended as hyperparameter tuning for performance optimization, but rather to demonstrate robustness and parameter effects on speed and source count. For competing methods, we used default parameters recommended in prior works and open-source implementations, which are already optimized (see Table 1 and Methods, Sec. 2.3). No tuning was performed on the evaluation set for any method, as stated in the manuscript.

**4. The evaluation and comparison is only on a single subject. It is unclear what degree of tuning is needed to deploy this to additional subjects which would impact computation time.**

MUelim was evaluated on both simulated and physiological datasets, and parameter sweeps demonstrate that the same algorithmic parameters worked well across all tested datasets. For the spinal cord injury participant demonstration, we used default parameter settings without prior tuning, demonstrating real-world applicability where parameter optimization is not feasible. We will clarify this in manuscript revision. However, we acknowledge that for deployment to new subjects, BSS filters would need recomputing, as these are subject-specific due to individual differences in anatomy, electrode placement, and muscle fiber organization.

**5. The spiking NN demo does not add much to the manuscript. It is unclear if similar results could be achieved with any spike extraction approach.**

The reviewer is correct that similar results can be achieved with other spike extraction approaches. However, the key contribution is demonstrating practical feasibility in real-world settings. MUelim's fast decomposition enables use in clinical or at-home applications where lengthy setup procedures are not practical. We prioritized demonstrating this with a spinal cord injury participant as part of a clinical trial with strict time constraints. Other methods requiring hours for decomposition would not be feasible in such sessions. This represents the first demonstration of this workflow in a clinical population, as described in Supp. Video S1.

**6. Why is uncertainty only reported in Table 1 for 1 method?**

Uncertainty was reported for MUelim because we ran the algorithm over multiple seeds for each parameter setting (main text, Sec. 2.3). For SCD, results were deterministic and for MUEdit, the manual nature of the tool precluded repeated runs. This is stated in the caption of Table 1 and in the main text (Sec. 3.1).

**7. Can you be more specific about how alternative methods were computationally optimized.**

For SCD, we used built-in GPU acceleration as recommended by the authors (main text, Sec. 2.3). For MUEdit, we followed the standard workflow with default parameters as described in documentation and open-source implementation. No custom optimizations were performed for any method, as stated in Methods (main text, Sec. 2.3).

**8. What is the time scaling of approaches with channels and additional motor units**

MUelim's computational complexity is primarily determined by the joint diagonalization step, which is performed on the extended data matrix. Specifically, the data is extended using R lagged versions of each channel, so the number of extended channels is C × R, where C is the number of original channels and R is the extension factor.

For the joint diagonalization step, the per-iteration computational cost is O(K(C×R)² + (C×R)³), where K is the number of matrices being diagonalized and C×R is the number of extended channels. For large C×R, the (C×R)³ term dominates, so the complexity is approximately O((C×R)³) per iteration. This scaling arises because the most expensive operation is matrix multiplications of size (C×R) × (C×R).

As channels or extension factor increases, decomposition time increases accordingly. However, MUelim's advantage becomes more pronounced with more motor unit sources, as it efficiently extracts many sources simultaneously rather than incrementally. We will add this computational complexity analysis to the manuscript revision.

**9. Where does the assumption of sparsity in the BSS fail**

Motor unit spike trains are inherently sparse, consisting of discrete action potentials separated by periods of inactivity, with firing rates typically in the 2-30 Hz range. The sparsity assumption may fail in rare cases of highly overlapping or synchronous firing among many motor units, or during pathological conditions with dense coordinated activity. However, under typical physiological conditions, motor unit population activity remains sparse, and BSS methods like MUelim are well suited.

**10. Can you give more details about the extracted MUAPs? Are their qualitative features that can be used to further convince the reader that these are 'real'**

The extracted MUAPs are real and physiologically plausible. MUAPs are electrical signatures generated by summation of action potentials from muscle fibers within a single motor unit. In our study, MUAPs were extracted using spike-triggered averaging of reconstructed EMG signal, which is a standard approach that effectively cancels noise and isolates the true underlying action potential waveform (main text, Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 2B).

The qualitative features of extracted MUAPs in our results are consistent with established physiological characteristics:

• Morphology: MUAPs typically exhibit a triphasic or biphasic shape. This morphology reflects the depolarization and repolarization phases of muscle fiber action potentials.

• Amplitude: Observed amplitudes are within the expected range for surface EMG, and vary according to the number and proximity of muscle fibers within the motor unit.

• Duration: MUAP durations are consistent with known physiological values, typically ranging from 5 to 30 ms, reflecting realistic muscle fiber conduction velocities and spatial dispersion.

• Firing rate: Extracted spike trains show realistic firing rates, typically in the range of 2-30 Hz that increase with force (main text, Fig. 2A).

• Simulated data validation: We validated MUelim on simulated EMG data with known ground truth, confirming that the extracted MUAPs and spike timings closely match the true underlying sources (main text, Sec. 3.1 and Supp. Fig. S2).

The clinical demonstration was designed as a proof-of-concept to establish the feasibility of real-time, closed-loop neuroprosthetic control using decomposed motor unit activity. While more complex tasks are an important direction for future work, the current results represent a significant advance, as previous methods required up to hours for decomposition, precluding any realistic real-time application outside of the research lab. We disagree with this characterization. MUelim combines established techniques (approximate joint diagonalization, extend-lag augmentation, iterative elimination) in a novel way that enables previously unattainable speed and practical use. The specific combination and implementation represents a significant algorithmic contribution that enables real-time applications not possible with existing methods. We note that NeurIPS guidelines emphasize that originality includes novel combinations of existing techniques that advance the field, which our work clearly demonstrates.

**4. Lack of theoretical complexity analysis: No formal time/space complexity or asymptotic runtime characterization is provided.**

We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. MUelim's computational complexity is primarily determined by the joint diagonalization step, which is performed on the extended data matrix. Specifically, the data is extended using R lagged versions of each channel, so the number of extended channels is C × R, where C is the number of original channels and R is the extension factor.

For the joint diagonalization step, the per-iteration computational cost is O(K(C×R)² + (C×R)³), where K is the number of matrices being diagonalized and C×R is the number of extended channels. For large C×R, the (C×R)³ term dominates, so the complexity is approximately O((C×R)³) per iteration. This scaling arises because the most expensive operation is matrix multiplications of size (C×R) × (C×R).

As channels or extension factor increases, decomposition time increases accordingly. However, MUelim's advantage becomes more pronounced with more motor unit sources, as it efficiently extracts many sources simultaneously rather than incrementally. We will add this computational complexity analysis to the manuscript revision.

**5. How do you choose the extension factor R?**

The choice of extension factor R is addressed empirically in the manuscript. As shown in Supplementary Figure S3 and main text Section 3.1, we performed a parameter sweep across R and τ (lag parameter), reporting that R=4 and τ=6 provided the best balance between number of decomposed sources and computation time. This represents a key algorithmic improvement over prior work by Negro et al. (2016), who recommends R = 1000/N (where N is the number of channels) with τ=1. By incorporating a larger lag parameter (τ=6), we achieve effective decomposition with a much smaller extension factor (R=4), which significantly reduces computational cost while maintaining performance. The method is robust across a range of R values, as demonstrated by our parameter sweeps. Adaptive or data-driven selection of R is an interesting direction for future work, but the current approach is effective and robust across the tested scenarios.

**6. Are there any more comparison methods available?**

We benchmarked MUelim against state-of-the-art open-source methods (MUEdit and SCD) using their recommended parameters and implementations (see Table 1 and Methods, Section 2.3). There are other methods in the field, such as DEMUSE, but these are commercially available and not accessible for independent benchmarking. 

Deep learning approaches for motor unit decomposition have also been proposed, but these require ground truth spike trains for training, which are obtained using convolutive BSS methods like the Negro method (MUEdit). Thus, deep learning models are not independent of BSS-based approaches and are only as good as the BSS methods used to generate their training data. This dependency makes comparison redundant, as the deep learning models inherit the limitations of the underlying BSS method used for ground truth generation.

The Negro et al. convolutive BSS approach (as implemented in MUEdit) is widely considered the gold standard for motor unit decomposition. One additional open-source package, emgdecomp (Formento 2021), implements an algorithm that is "heavily based on Negro et al". We chose to use MUEdit for comparison as it is the newer tool and comes from the original research group. Thus, our benchmarking covers the most relevant and rigorous open-source baselines available to the community for motor unit decomposition.

**7. In Table 1, is the extension factor R seriously affecting the response time? Increasing R leads to longer or shorter decomposition time but also more decomposed sources?**

Yes, the extension factor R significantly affects decomposition time. As shown in Table 1 and Supplementary Figure S3, increasing R generally increases the number of decomposed sources but also increases decomposition time due to the larger extended data matrix. This follows the O((C×R)³) computational complexity we described earlier. The parameter sweep results provide guidance for selecting R to balance speed and source yield, with R=4 providing an optimal trade-off for our applications.

**8. In equation (1), dimensions of each component do not correspond to each other.**

We thank the reviewer for identifying this dimensional inconsistency. This is due to a notational oversight. We framed the BSS problem using standard literature convention but did not update the dimensions to match our implementation where samples are along axis 0. We will correct the equation in the manuscript revision to ensure proper dimensional alignment.

summary.value: This paper presents MUelim, a novel algorithm designed for real-time motor unit decomposition from high-density electromyography (HD-EMG) signals. The core contribution is an efficient method that leverages approximate joint diagonalization combined with a novel extend-lag data augmentation procedure to extract motor unit activity quickly and accurately. The method is validated on both simulated and physiological HD-EMG data and is shown to outperform state-of-the-art techniques in terms of decomposition speed—up to 3,700% faster—while maintaining comparable accuracy. MUelim is also demonstrated in a clinical setting, enabling an individual with spinal cord injury to control a neuroprosthetic device in real-time via decoded motor intent, showcasing its potential in assistive neurotechnology.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

1. Efficiency: MUelim offers significant speed improvements over current methods, making it suitable for real-time applications.
2. Clinical relevance: Demonstrated utility in a real clinical trial, enabling intention-driven control of a neuroprosthetic device.
3. High accuracy: Achieved nearly perfect spike timing detection in simulated data (99.93% accuracy).
4. Robust evaluation pipeline: Includes parameter sweeps (extension factor, lag, estimator types), detailed algorithm validation, and real-world application.
5. Integration with spiking neural networks: Enables low-power, event-driven decoding for future neuromorphic applications.

Weaknesses:

1. Limited dataset diversity: Only tested on non-invasive HD-EMG; not validated on intramuscular EMG or broader subject populations.
2. Simplified tasks: Real-world clinical task is relatively simple, potentially limiting generalization to more complex motor intentions.
3. Algorithmic novelty: While practical, the core techniques are adapted from prior work rather than invented anew.
4. Lack of theoretical complexity analysis: No formal time/space complexity or asymptotic runtime characterization is provided.

summary.value: This paper shows a method for accurate and efficient motor unit decomposition called MUelim. The authors demonstrate motor unit decomposition for simulated EMG data, an able-bodied individual, and an individual with spinal cord injury.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
* Significant speed improvement of 3700% over an alternative method
* Evaluates motor unit decomposition with a user with spinal cord injury and uses this for real-time inference for FES
* Shows similar SNR and number of motor units decomposed as the baseline methods

Weaknesses
* Does not compare with public datasets for motor unit decomposition
* Limited machine learning evaluation. ML evaluation is with a single participant in what seems to be a single trial for three similar pick and place tasks task. 
* Even with an able-bodied individual, only a single individual is tested for motor unit decomposition 
* Does not compare with other machine learning preprocessing methods for ML task (e.g. classification on raw signals, RMS signals, or time-frequency transforms).

questions.value:
* How do these motor unit decomposition methods perform with public datasets?
* How useful is motor unit decomposition for downstream tasks such as classification of hand open, hand close, and rest compared to other preprocessing methods?
* ASIA D usually means significant motor function is retained by the user. How much was the FES needed to restore function for this user for the pick and place tasks demonstrated?

summary.value:
- The authors introduce a new algorithm MUelim for decomposing high-density surface EMG into the motor units that generated the signals.
- The algorithm shows great speed improvements (up to 3700%) versus the current state-of-the-art methods
- They demonstrated the usefulness of the decomposition by having a participant with SCI control their hand through FES by decoding the intention (hand open, close, rest) from the extracted MUAPs using a spiking neural network.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
- The presented algorithm works fast and builds on existing literature
- Having a fast and accurate algorithm for MUAP decomposition can be very valuable for a number of other projects
- They show that the method works in simulated data, which is key to understand the behavior of the novel method.
- They test it on a real scenario and show that it works and can be useful to extract control signals in a participant with SCI.
- Paper is well written and leads the reader nicely through the methods and the results.

Weaknesses:
- During simulation, it would be good to have a comparison with other methods, making sure that the results are similar. Also, please add a figure to the main text related to simulation: making sure that the novel method can detect all sources and has results similar to existing methods is a key results of the paper. Finally, you discuss that one of the key parts of the method allowed to get more sources than the available channels, but you do not test this in simulation.
- You mention in the paper that you were able to use the method online in the clinical setting. However, the time for decomposition you showed was in minutes. Did you pre-compute the decomposition and then use the forward matrix online? This needs an important clarification, as one of your motivation points talks about being able to use this online, and this may not be a big difference with existing methods.
- The task you tested in the clinical setting is probably not the best way to motivate this method: from the video in the supplemental, I can see the participant had quite a bit of residual movement, which means that you could do the same task just by processing the full EMG. The method would be better motivated in cases in which you are interested in the MUAPs individually: maybe more neuroscience related questions, or tasks in which participants are instructed to control specific MUAPs.

questions.value:
Methods:
1. Paragraph on how the MUAP waveforms are extracted (lines 181-186) is not very clear. Please add more details into how this process works.
2. You mention in the introduction that the addition of time-delayed extensions prior to joint diagonalizations helps with potentially extracting more sources than channels. However, in section 2.3 you only evaluate cases in which there are many more channels than sources. What happens when the number of sources is higher than the number of channels? Also, please compare the simulation results you got with existing methods (such as MUedit and SCD). 
3. In section 2.4, please add how much residual movement the participant had available. Were they able to open and close their hand by themselves?
4. The manuscript would greatly benefit from some diagram of the training procedure and inference during the neuroprosthetic experiment, potentially as an addition to Figure 3.
5. Was the EMG decomposition done before starting the inference experiment? If so, how did you decompose the EMG signal in real-time? Please clarify. If you are pre-computing the forward filters, please clarify.

Results:
1. Please add a figure to the main text with the results from the simulation experiment, as it can give key insights into whether the proposed method is working as expected. At the beginning of the results section you cite Figure 1, but that doesn’t really contain simulation results.
2. Make sure that the units of Figure 2B (especially the right plot) are correct. 
3. Figure 2C is not mentioned in the main text: what is the message you are trying to convey with it?
4. In Table 1, why do you show variability for MUelim but not for the other methods? Also, add a discussion on what the expected number of motor units should be, to better understand the results.
5. How does the per-bin accuracy looks like if you use the full non-decomposed EMG rather than motor units? I would imagine that it would be much higher performance, but that would depend on how much residual movement the participant may have. Please add a few sentences to the limitations paragraph related to this method in this participant.
6. Mark the transition between rest and hand open in Figure 3A
7. Figure 3D probably has wrong units.

Discussion:
1. In lines 322-323 you claim “MUelim achieves similar or greater source yield with 323 substantially reduced computation time, supporting its use in closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems”. However, the computation times you show are in the order of minutes. If you are pre-computing the forward filters please clarify and tone down the claim.

If these comments and questions are addressed, I’ll increase my score.

summary.value: This manuscript introduces an approach MUEdit for decomposing motor unit action potentials from HD-sEMG. The proposed method uses a combination of joint diagonalization and expansion of the domain by time-lagging to identify motor unit sources and identify more sources than sEMG channels in a computationally efficient manner. They show successful recovery in synthetic data. They compare to a small set of alternative methods on a single subject, showing improvements in speed compared to alternative approaches. They show a demo using the extracted MUAPs to drive a spiking neural network in a spinal cord injury patient.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
The algorithm appears to be novel and show some advantages in speed/computation time compared to other approaches. 
There are several contemporary alternative approaches benchmarked. 

Weaknesses
* Evaluations and baselines are unconvincing and limited
* The advantages of the algorithm is not made especially clear, and its performance in different data regimes (e.g. sparse, dense, scaling with channel counts) is not shown. There is not a set of ablations that makes clear how different algorithmic properties and features factor into computational savings and data quality (e.g. removing time lag, approximations of joint diagonalization).

questions.value:
* The synthetic data experiments are too easy, as the algorithm achieves perfect performance. Competing methods are not benchmarked on synthetic data, which is the only regime that has a ground truth, so its unclear exactly how these are compared. 

* The proposed algorithm is benchmarked in Figure 2 with extensive hyperparameter tuning as shown in Supplementary Figure 3 and then compared to alternative algorithms using open source hyperparameters. Its not clear if these hyperparameters were tuned on the evaluation set, and how the competing algorithms would perform with additional hyperparameter tuning. 

* The evaluation and comparison is only on a single subject. It is unclear what degree of tuning is needed to deploy this to additional subjects which would impact computation time. 

* The spiking NN demo does not add much to the manuscript. It is unclear if similar results could be achieved with any spike extraction approach. 

Minor

* Why is uncertainty only reported in Table 1 for 1 method?

* Can you be more specific about how alternative methods were computationally optimized. 

* What is the time scaling of approaches with channels and additional motor units

* Where does the assumption of sparsity in the BSS fail

* Can you give more details about the extracted MUAPs? Are their qualitative features that can be used to further convince the reader that these are 'real'

title.value: Decomposing motor units through elimination for real-time intention driven assistive neurotechnology

TLDR.value: We introduce MUelim, an algorithm for efficient motor unit decomposition that uses approximate joint diagonalization with a subtractive approach to rapidly identify motor units for advanced neuroprosthetic control.

abstract.value: Extracting neural signals at the single motor neuron level provides an optimal control signal for neuroprosthetic applications. However, current algorithms to decompose motor units from high-density electromyography (HD-EMG) are time-consuming and inconsistent, limiting their application to controlled scenarios in a research setting. We introduce MUelim, an algorithm for efficient motor unit decomposition that uses approximate joint diagonalization with a subtractive approach to rapidly identify and refine candidate sources. The algorithm incorporates an extend-lag procedure to augment data for enhanced source separability prior to diagonalization. By systematically iterating and eliminating redundant or noisy sources, MUelim achieves high decomposition accuracy while significantly reducing computational complexity, making it well-suited for real-time applications. We validate MUelim by demonstrating its ability to extract motor units in both simulated and physiological HD-EMG grid data. Across six healthy participants performing ramp and maximum voluntary contraction paradigms, MUelim achieves up to a 36$\times$ speed increase compared to existing state-of-the-art methods while decomposing a similar number of high signal-to-noise sources. Furthermore, we showcase a real-world application of MUelim in a clinical setting in which an individual with spinal cord injury controlled an EMG-driven neuroprosthetic to perform functional tasks. We demonstrate the ability to decode motor intent in real-time using a spiking neural network trained on the decomposed motor unit spike trains to trigger functional electrical stimulation patterns that evoke hand movements during task practice therapy. We show that motor unit-based decoding enables nuanced motor control, highlighting the potential of MUelim to advance assistive neurotechnology and rehabilitation through precise, intention-driven neuroprosthetic systems.

abstract.description: Abstract of paper. Add TeX formulas using the following formats: $In-line Formula$ or $$Block Formula$$.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15)

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and ensure all material is anonymized. The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22)

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/ ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.

LLM_usage.description: This checklist collects statistical information on how NeurIPS authors use Generative AI (e.g., LLMs) in manuscript preparation. Responses are confidential and will not be shared with reviewers, area chairs, or senior chairs. The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.
